summary.text: An 18-year-old male with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after being struck by a motor vehicle while walking. He had a Glasgow Coma Score of 3 at the paramedic assessment and a revised score of 8 on hospital arrival, with tachycardia, tachypnea, normotension, dilated pupils with delayed light response, a blood alcohol concentration of 0.21%, and hematomas, bruises and abrasions on the upper abdomen and chest wall.

Sonography showed intra-abdominal free fluid and a pelvic hematoma measuring 9×5 cm. Whole-body CT showed contusion and laceration of the upper lobe of the right lung, bilateral pneumothorax, bilateral first rib fractures and a C7 transverse process fracture. The cervical injury resulted in dissection and occlusion of the left vertebral artery, and the contralateral vertebral artery was hypoplastic.

A chest tube was placed for the left-sided pneumothorax. Hypotension, a hemoglobin decline from 120 to 91 g/L and active intra-abdominal bleeding led to urgent exploratory laparotomy, where a grade 3 laceration of the eighth liver segment was controlled with direct sutures and a hemostatic sponge. A Philadelphia cervical collar was applied postoperatively. After regaining consciousness he reported a right visual field deficit, and follow-up head CT showed signs of acute ischemia. Therapeutic enoxaparin was initiated once bleeding risk was considered acceptably low.

He recovered well without significant complications, the chest tube was removed a few days later, and the subsequent course was uneventful. He was discharged on 300 mg of acetylsalicylic acid as chronic therapy, later reduced to 100 mg. At the final follow-up 6 months after discharge the homonymous hemianopsia persisted; MR angiography showed healing of the vascular injury with slight arterial wall irregularity, and stationary encephalomalacia was present in the ischemia-affected regions.
